disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms within three months of an identifiable stressor, with distress that is out of proportion to the stressor or associated with significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The presentation can include anxious, depressed, or mixed mood changes, as well as maladaptive behaviors, but does not meet full criteria for another specific mental disorder and is not merely an exacerbation of a preexisting condition. Symptoms typically resolve within six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended, though it can become chronic if the stressor persists. It is differentiated from normal stress reactions by the degree of impairment and from disorders such as major depressive disorder or generalized anxiety disorder by its time-limited course and clear temporal relationship to a specific stressor.

narrative.personality: Curious, sociable, and creative, Araceli is usually easygoing and resourceful but tends to rely on last-minute bursts of effort to meet obligations.
narrative.stressor: About three months ago, Araceli’s company went through a sudden restructuring in which two front-desk colleagues were laid off and she was informally expected to absorb much of their workload without a clear pay increase or timeline. At the same time, a new supervisor with a highly detail-oriented, perfectionistic style began closely monitoring her performance, criticizing her informal workflow "hacks" and pushing her to enroll in evening classes to finish her diploma if she wanted to keep advancing. Initially, Araceli tried to treat it as a challenge, staying late and leaning on coffee-fueled sprints to keep up while still squeezing in live music outings and church volunteering, but over several weeks the constant pressure and lack of structure around the new expectations began to overwhelm her usual relaxed adaptability. As small mistakes at work started to affect her confidence and she found herself struggling to keep the office running smoothly and maintain her outside interests, she became worried about her job stability and, at the urging of a church mentor who noticed the change in her functioning, agreed to seek psychiatric help.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like ever since all the changes at work, I’m not handling the stress in a healthy way anymore.

narrative.personality: Gary is a methodical, data-driven problem solver who values balance, quiet reflection, and cooperative relationships in both work and home life.
narrative.stressor: Roughly two and a half months ago, Gary’s spouse disclosed that they were seriously considering a trial separation after a series of unresolved disagreements about starting a family and Gary’s long work hours on a major organizational restructuring project. Accustomed to approaching problems analytically, he initially threw himself into reading relationship books and tracking "metrics" of their communication, trying to negotiate solutions while still meeting high expectations at work. As the weeks went on and his spouse began spending more nights away at a friend’s place, the uncertainty at home started to bleed into his normally steady performance; he found himself second-guessing decisions, avoiding social board game nights with friends, and skipping outings like Red Rock hikes that had previously grounded him. When his supervisor gently noted a drop in his engagement and his spouse suggested counseling as a condition for reconsidering the relationship, Gary recognized that his usual self-reliant coping strategies were no longer sufficient and sought psychiatric evaluation to better manage his reaction to the relationship crisis.
narrative.chief_complaint: Ever since my marriage hit this rough patch, I’m reacting to the stress in ways that don’t feel like me and it’s starting to affect my work and home life.

narrative.personality: Tim is an energetic, improvisational caregiver who thrives on spontaneity, social connection, and hands-on activities but dislikes rigid structure and detailed planning.
narrative.stressor: About two months ago, after weeks of ignoring nagging fatigue and shortness of breath, Tim was unexpectedly hospitalized and diagnosed with a chronic cardiac condition that required medication, dietary changes, and limits on physically strenuous activity. For someone used to leading lively group sessions at the senior center, bowling in a league, and hauling lumber for woodworking projects, the abrupt shift to being a "patient" with restrictions felt like a profound blow to his identity and independence. He initially tried to shrug it off with humor and keep up his usual pace, but as his cardiologist warned him about overexertion and his employer temporarily reassigned him to less active duties, he began to feel increasingly cornered by the lifestyle changes and struggled to adjust his day-to-day routines. When his difficulty following medical advice and changes in his reliability at work started to create tension with colleagues and risked his position at the senior center, a supportive supervisor and his primary care physician encouraged him to see a psychiatrist to address how he was coping with the new health limitations.
narrative.chief_complaint: Since I found out about this heart issue, I just haven’t been dealing with it well and it’s really messing with how I handle my life and my job.
